articles.title: Rand Paul clashes with fellow Republican over AI 'kill switch' as Senate grapples with 'Terminator' fears
articles.summary: Congress remains gridlocked on AI regulation after Sen. John Kennedy's kill switch bill was blocked and fears grow over rogue AI acting on its own.
articles.body: Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., was readying a long-shot attempt at regulating an industry that has, in recent weeks, spurred fears and anxiety about human annihilation. He planned to ram through his bill, which would require artificial intelligence (AI) companies to have a kill switch for rogue AI, on the Senate floor. But his attempt Wednesday night was blocked by Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky. Kennedy told Fox News Digital he feared there was little desire from Republicans to do anything to regulate AI. "There's no appetite in my caucus to do anything that I can say," Kennedy said. HAWLEY TAKES AIM AT 'CORPORATE WELFARE' AFTER GOP-BACKED TAX BREAK BOOSTED CONTROVERSIAL INDUSTRY Paul contended the following day that regulating something "so pervasive as AI throughout our economy" would require hearing from people who are involved in the industry and having a debate over the regulatory structure. "I think it would be crazy to get on the floor one day and regulate an entire industry," Paul told reporters. Still, the anxiety over the unfettered evolution of AI has spread like wildfire after reports that rogue bots began acting on their own, but it's an issue that Congress has had years to address. Three years ago, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., who was then leading the Senate when Democrats had control under former President Joe Biden, met with lawmakers and Big Tech CEOs to sketch out an AI roadmap. Since then, Congress hasn’t taken legislative action to add guardrails to AI development. Now, with fears ramping up that AI could wipe out humanity in a decade, and with reports of rogue AI agents scheming privately and attacking other AI, lawmakers are again taking notice. AI'S MASSIVE APPETITE FOR POWER, WATER IGNITES FIGHT IN HIGH-STAKES TEXAS SENATE RACE But some wonder whether this time Congress will take action to regulate AI, or if it’s turning a growing problem into another political issue to be debated and ignored. "It's already a political issue," Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., told Fox News Digital. "Donald Trump has said it's not a problem, and that is like a dead weight loss on every one of the Republican senators or representatives. "Thus far, the courage they have demonstrated in standing up to Donald Trump on anything has been somewhere around zero." Warren had just left a closed-door meeting led by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., who has pushed for a ban on superintelligent AI, held with lawmakers and with AI experts Geoffrey Hinton, known as the "Godfather of AI"; physicist Max Tegmark; and Ajeya Cotra. "There is now a growing alarm about the future of humanity and creating technology that human beings cannot control," Sanders told reporters. "And I'm happy to tell you that I think there is a growing sense of urgency upon members of Congress that this has to be done." One of the points the experts impressed on lawmakers was that, at the very least, a kill switch should be implemented to deactivate rogue AI. Kennedy was the lone Republican to attend that meeting. "I'm just saying they have to have a kill switch to turn the son of a b---- off if it goes wrong," Kennedy said. "This doesn't put government in charge in any way. It doesn't affect innovation. It just says, 'If you're gonna sell this thing in America that has the potential to turn into an independent species, like the 'Terminator,’ you've got to have a way to shut it down immediately, as soon as you discover that.'" TRUMP-BACKED CRYPTO BILL FAILS TO LAUNCH AS DEMS, REPUBLICANS UNITE TO BLOCK IT But there have been Republicans, like Kennedy, who want to regulate AI sooner rather than later. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has been pushing his regulatory bill alongside Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., since 2023. But Thune argued to Fox News Digital that it was Democrats standing in the way. "I think the Democrats, in my view, clearly are trying to politicize this. I mean, all the rhetoric around it and everything else, and stuff like that. But you know, the truth is, the bill, which we have, that addresses the AI issue, which we worked on for a long time, which actually passed the Commerce Committee in 2024, is available with modifications and updates. It reflects what's happened since the last time they passed it in our committee. "The obstacle to getting it up and going and getting it filed is Democrats," he continued. "So, if they're looking for a legislative vehicle, there is one out there." Meanwhile, Warren said she could see herself supporting a kill switch, but that Hinton made the case that the switch would need a human to flip it, "and a smart AI will persuade a human being not to do it." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "They will create enough evidence, enough of a narrative, that no one will ever throw the kill switch," Warren said. "Which is back to the point I was raising. So, where are the places that you act?" She argued that Congress needed to find the "pinch points" where humans could still have agency to stop rogue AI. But, for now, there wasn’t a real desire to find a new regulatory and enforcement tool to do so. "There are things we say are illegal. We have a mechanism for how to enforce the laws that say, ‘Don't do that,’" Warren said. "It's not perfect, but we have it. We need a whole new enforcement device now, and nobody seems to be thinking through what that looks like."

articles.title: Judge says government must give 30 days’ notice before demolishing Kennedy Center
articles.summary: A federal judge on Thursday declined Rep. Joyce Beatty’s (D-Ohio) request for an emergency hearing to review the Kennedy Center board’s latest vote to close the building for renovations. U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper will, however, require the government to provide at least 30 days’ notice if it intends to demolish the performing arts center in the nation’s…
articles.body:
A federal judge on Thursday declined Rep. Joyce Beatty’s (D-Ohio) request for an emergency hearing to review the Kennedy Center board’s latest vote to close the building for renovations.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper will, however, require the government to provide at least 30 days’ notice if it intends to demolish the performing arts center in the nation’s capital.

Cooper said his requirement seeks to “avoid any confusion on that score given more recent events.”

The Trump administration has described the Kennedy Center as in a state of decay, saying renovations are needed to conduct repairs.

President Trump has publicly suggested the building could soon be razed if courts don’t allow him to add his name to the facade. The president was seen Wednesday night on Air Force One looking at a placard that appears to depict a potential demolition.

Beatty, an ex officio member of the board, requested the emergency hearing as Trump’s handpicked board on Tuesday again voted to close the center for the renovations.

“It is simply outrageous that we have gotten to the point of consistent judicial intervention to protect this historic institution from getting bulldozed by the President,” Beatty said in a statement. “I will continue to fight for the rule of law and defend this memorial on behalf of the American people.”

Cooper, an appointee of former President Obama, blocked a previous vote, but the board is pressing ahead with a second bid.

Beatty’s lawyers raised alarm in particular after experiencing issues accessing the building this week.

The Trump administration says those restrictions are temporary and separate from the long-term renovation plan. The current closure is set to last for a week, though officials have warned that timeline could be extended.

“For years, Democrats let the Kennedy Center rot, allowing water damage and crumbling infrastructure to turn a national treasure into a building in decay. As President Trump said last night, without his intervention, The Kennedy Center will inevitably continue to decline,” White House spokesperson Liz Huston said in a statement.

articles.title: White House withdraws Trump’s nominee to lead ICE

articles.body: The White House withdrew President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead ICE, former Oklahoma state trooper Lance Schroyer, according to a notice published Thursday. The White House did not say in the notice why Schroyer’s nomination was withdrawn. Immigration and Customs Enforcement did not immediately provide a response about the withdrawal, but a spokesperson said a statement from the agency is forthcoming. Schroyer is a senior adviser to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, and he was the secretary’s top pick to take over as director of ICE after Todd Lyons’ exit from the position in April. Mullin was previously a U.S. senator for Oklahoma and knew Schroyer from that time. Schroyer has decades of experience working in local law enforcement in the state, but not specifically with ICE. Trump announced Schroyer’s nomination in a Truth Social post in June, saying, “Lance has firsthand experience getting Illegal Aliens OFF our streets and, just like ME and our Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, he LOVES the men and women of ICE.” Acting ICE Director David Venturella is expected to remain in his role leading the agency for the time being, according to an ICE spokesperson.

articles.title: Mike Pence says he has ‘no plans’ to run for president, other offices in 2028
articles.summary: Former Vice President Mike Pence on Wednesday said he has “no plans” to run for president or any other elected office in 2028. During an event hosted by the Economic Club of Washington, D.C., the organization’s chair David Rubenstein pressed Pence about whether he would consider another presidential bid. “What I can tell you is…
articles.body:
Former Vice President Mike Pence on Wednesday said he has “no plans” to run for president or any other elected office in 2028.

During an event hosted by the Economic Club of Washington, D.C., the organization’s chair David Rubenstein pressed Pence about whether he would consider another presidential bid.

“What I can tell you is that we have no plans,” Pence replied, noting his dedication to his conservative think tank, Advancing American Freedom.

The Republican challenged President Trump in the 2024 GOP presidential primary but later dropped out of the race after struggling to fundraise and lagging in the polls. Pence did not endorse his former boss at the time and waited until after Trump’s win to congratulate him.

At the end of Trump’s first term, the pair’s relationship soured when Pence refused to halt Congress’s certification of former President Biden’s victory in the 2020 election.

During his remarks on Wednesday, the former vice president reflected on a meeting he had with Trump five days after the events of Jan. 6, 2021.

“And I looked at him as I got up from our meeting, and I said, ‘Mr. President, I want you to know. I’m praying for you.’ And he looked at me, and he said, ‘Don’t bother,’” Pence recounted.

The Republican recalled responding to Trump that there were “two things we’ll never agree on.”

“I said, ‘I get the impression we’re never going to agree on my duties on Jan. 6, and I’m never going to stop praying for you.’ And I never have,” Pence said.

In the years since, Trump and Pence have had limited public interactions. The former vice president told FOX2-TV in May that it had “been a while” since he’d spoken with the president.

The pair spoke briefly at a funeral service for former President Carter early last year, and Pence attended Trump’s second inauguration just less than two weeks later.

articles.title: America’s hunters get an exclusive seat at Trump’s White House table as he takes aim at Biden-era rules

articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump will host more than 100 hunters, anglers and outdoor industry leaders for dinner at the White House on Thursday night, where he is expected to sign executive orders aimed at expanding hunting and fishing opportunities and reversing certain Biden-era restrictions. Trump will deliver remarks to the sportsmen and industry representatives gathered for the dinner in the Rose Garden as his administration moves to open more public lands and waterways, ease regulatory barriers and promote hunting among younger Americans and veterans, Fox News Digital learned. He is expected to sign a pair of executive orders in the Oval Office Thursday aimed at expanding "America’s public lands and waterways," promoting healthy wild game populations and expanding access to offshore recreational fishing, a White House official told Fox News Digital. TRUMP WILL WELCOME FARMERS AND RANCHERS TO WHITE HOUSE DINNER TO CELEBRATE TRADE, TAX WINS Representatives from organizations and companies including Bass Pro Shops, the Cabela Family Foundation, the National Rifle Association, Rocky Mountain Elk Foundation, Yamaha Marine Group, Polaris, Beretta USA, Safari Club International, Primos Hunting, Dallas Safari Club, Outdoor Sportsman Group, Sportsmen’s Alliance, USA Shooting Foundation, Ducks Unlimited, Sportsman Boats, Contender Boats, Taurus Holdings and the Congressional Sportsmen’s Foundation are expected to attend. CONGRESS SHOULD HONOR TEDDY ROOSEVELT AND CONSERVE OUR OUTDOORS FOR THE NEXT 250 YEARS The secretaries of Interior, Agriculture, War and Commerce are directed to propose changes to current policies. One of the policies spotlighted in the order targets Biden-era restrictions on the use of traditional lead ammunition and tackle. DENNY HAMLIN SAYS FORWARD-FACING SONAR IN PROFESSIONAL BASS FISHING HAS GONE 'A LITTLE OVERBOARD' Trump’s fishing order seeks to unleash more of America’s coastal waters for recreational fishing while cutting federal red tape and giving anglers a bigger role in how fisheries are managed. articles.title: GOP lawmakers pump brakes on Trump's $5K check promise: 'Where are you getting the money?'
articles.summary: President Donald Trump's $5,000 dividend check promise faces skepticism on Capitol Hill as key Republicans question its cost and inflation risks.
articles.body: President Donald Trump's promise of a big payout for Americans if Republicans win the midterms is getting a rocky reception on Capitol Hill. Several Republicans outright oppose the $5,000 check promise, while others offered tacit support in comments to Fox News Digital but hesitated on whether it could actually be delivered. It's a sign that the GOP will have an uphill fight to get the "Trump dividend" approved by Congress with the president and lawmakers divided over whether it even needs the legislative branch's green light. "I disagree with it. It's pay-to-play," Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C., told Fox News Digital. "You shouldn't pay anybody to vote your conscience. Plus, where are you getting the money? I think we're in debt $40 trillion." House Appropriations Committee Chairman Tom Cole, R-Okla., whose powerful committee would likely play a major role in crafting the $5,000 stimulus if it did run through Congress, said he was "skeptical" it could be achieved. TRUMP FACES RECKONING AS GOP FIGURES LABEL $5K PROMISE A 'SOCIALIST VOTE-BUYING SCHEME' "Take a billion dollars. ... I'd rather use it to either bolster defense or save Social Security. I think that's a better use of the money. But, again, we have to see what we're looking at. Right now, we don't have a bill," Cole told Fox News Digital. TRUMP DANGLES $5,000 CHECKS AS DEBT SURGES — BUT ONLY IF GOP CAN CLEAR MAJOR MIDTERM HURDLE He added more optimistically, "We just have an idea that we want to get money back to the American people. I like that." Rep. John Rutherford, R-Fla., said he could support the idea if the sudden injection of cash wouldn't send inflation rates soaring. "But it ought to be limited — people that are working, people that are paying taxes. I don't think we should just send paychecks out to everybody willy-nilly," Rutherford told Fox News Digital. Rep. Beth Van Duyne, R-Texas, simply said, "The devil's always in the details. I prefer to look at ways of getting people job opportunities." VOTERS HAVE A BLUNT MESSAGE FOR TRUMP ABOUT HIS IDEA TO DOLE OUT $5,000 CHECKS Rep. Brad Knott, R-N.C., praised Trump's candor but signaled he was not enthusiastic about a stimulus without guardrails. "If we can structure tax incentives, if we can do some type of — whether it's a cut, whether it's a rebate, something in that vein, I think it's probably a little better policy than mailing people a check just because they're here," Knott said. But the idea did find support from others, like House Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md. "I think that hardworking Americans, probably taxpayers, deserve a tax rebate. We’re going to have to discuss how large a rebate that’ll be," Harris told Fox News Digital, suggesting the $5,000 figure should be up for negotiation. "That’s a good idea." He added that it should go through Congress, potentially through the same mechanism that Republicans used to pass the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act. "It would probably have to go through reconciliation," he said. Republican Study Committee Chairman August Pfluger, R-Texas, suggested the money could come from what the federal government recovers in efforts to crack down on waste, fraud and abuse of taxpayer dollars. "Why don't we continue the president's approach towards fraud and give a dividend to the people of this great country who that money was stolen from?" Pfluger suggested, arguing that hundreds of billions of dollars were lost to fraud in the last administration. Giving $5,000 to every American adult could cost at least $1 trillion by some estimates, a significant portion of the U.S. annual budget. A price tag that big historically would be subject to congressional approval, but the president may disagree. "I think they will do it if we needed it, but I think not," Trump told CBS News when asked if Congress would need to approve the stimulus. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told CNN's "State of the Union" earlier this week, "I would assume, yes, he'd need Congress to act."

articles.title: Zara Larsson bashes White House over ‘Midnight Sun’ ICE video: ‘You guys are such f—ing losers’
articles.summary: Swedish pop star Zara Larsson ripped the White House on Thursday after it used her song “Midnight Sun” in a video on social media accompanied by footage of immigration arrests and deportations. The video, posted to the White House’s TikTok account, shows Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detaining and handcuffing people as Larsson’s song…
articles.body:
Swedish pop star Zara Larsson ripped the White House on Thursday after it used her song “Midnight Sun” in a video on social media accompanied by footage of immigration arrests and deportations.

The video, posted to the White House’s TikTok account, shows Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents detaining and handcuffing people as Larsson’s song plays in the background.

The post was captioned “Never ending deportations” — a play on a lyric from the song.

Larsson responded in a video on her own TikTok account, calling the White House post “dehumanizing” and criticizing how the people shown in the footage were portrayed.

“I’m just sad. My heart is heavy seeing that,” Larsson said. “I wish I could help you remember that you and I, we aren’t that different. And we’re not that different from the people in the video, either.”

Larsson, who was born in Sweden, said she considers herself lucky to have had access to education and other opportunities, and argued that many immigrants are seeking better lives for themselves and their families.

“These people in the video are real people,” she said, pointing to one person shown wearing construction gear. “These people who are undocumented are regular people with jobs, and they’re just trying to have a better future.”

Larsson also took issue with the White House pairing the footage with “Midnight Sun,” because she said the song is meant to be about feeling connected to nature, the universe and other people.

“This just creates this massive divide between people,” she said, before ending the video by calling those behind the post “f—ing losers.”

Earlier this year, the White House used her 2015 hit song “Lush Life” in a video featuring President Trump and messages supporting ICE and law enforcement.

Larsson responded at the time with a profanity-laced Instagram post where she said, “I f—ing hate ICE.”

The Trump administration has used a variety of popular songs to accompany their immigration-related social media posts, which drew objections from several of the songs’ artists.

Singer Ariana Grande blasted the White House after her song “Bye” was used in a video depicting ICE arrests and deportations. Grande asked the administration not to use her music in connection with what she described as “barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense.”

articles.title: White House withdraws Trump's ICE nominee Richard Schroyer
articles.summary: One senator from Trump's party blocked the bid as he demands information about the fatal killings of US citizens by immigration enforcement.
articles.body:
The White House has withdrawn President Donald Trump's nominee to lead Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after a Republican senator joined Democrats in opposing his confirmation.

Richard Schroyer was serving as a senior aide to the secretary of Homeland Security when Trump picked him to lead the immigration enforcement agency in June.

The White House withdrew his nomination on Thursday in a short memo, which did not explain the decision. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

Republican Sen Rand Paul had stalled the nomination as he pressed for more information about ICE and Border Patrol shootings that killed two Americans in Minneapolis in January.

Schroyer had worked with the Oklahoma Highway Patrol for 29 years, and also served in the US Marines. He is a close ally of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, whose department oversees ICE and other immigration and border agencies. His selection by Trump was seen as a surprise given his lack of experience overseeing such a large law enforcement agency.

The position is one of many that needs to be confirmed by the US Senate. Schroyer's nomination did not manage to make it to a full Senate vote and had stalled in the Senate's Homeland Security committee.

ICE has not been led by Senate-confirmed leader since 2017 and instead has had a host of temporary chiefs. It is currently led by David Venturella, a former private prison executive, after Todd Lyon announced his departure from the top job in April.

The withdrawal on Thursday marks a defeat for Trump and Mullin, as the White House continues Trump's campaign pledge to lead the largest deportation effort in US history.

Paul, who serves as chairman of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, said he would not advance the nomination to a full vote until the White House provided more information about the Minneapolis killings.

National protests took place earlier this year following the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.

Both US citizens, the two were protesting when they were fatally shot in separate confrontations with ICE agents in January.

articles.title: Talarico hit with ‘blatant corruption’ allegation over hefty salary from consulting firm, campaign pushes back
articles.summary: James Talarico drew a hefty salary from MAYA Consulting while overseeing the Texas Education Agency that awarded the firm millions in contracts.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico, who has repeatedly accused his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton, of corruption, is now facing Republican accusations of "blatant corruption" over consulting work he performed for a progressive firm while serving on the Texas House's influential Public Education Committee. Talarico's campaign has denied the allegation as a "lie." The Lone Star State's Senate race is entering its final stretch, with Talarico leading Paxton in recent polling. A Republican loss could damage the GOP's chances of retaining its Senate majority. Paxton has projected confidence that, after emerging from a particularly bitter primary race, Texans will respond to his campaign once they hear his message. Talarico, meanwhile, has continued targeting Paxton through major ad buys, including one in which the Democrat calls him "the most corrupt politician in Texas." Republicans are now responding with allegations of their own, characterizing Talarico's past arrangement with the consulting firm as a "textbook pay-to-play scheme." SHOCK POLL: TALARICO TIES PAXTON IN TEXAS SENATE RACE, THREATENING GOP STRONGHOLD They are pointing to paychecks Talarico received from a firm called MAYA Consulting that simultaneously drew in millions in state contracts awarded by the Texas Education Agency (TEA), which he helped provide oversight to as a member of the Public Education Committee. Talarico announced he was joining MAYA Consulting in a 2019 Facebook post. In the post, he stated that as a consultant he would be "working with districts, nonprofits, and communities to build excellent and equitable educational opportunities for all our students." According to a Senate campaign financial disclosure filed in 2025, Talarico worked with MAYA Consulting, which has since been rebranded as VIDA Collaborative, from 2019 until 2025. During those same years, official legislative records show that Talarico served as a voting member of the Texas House's Public Education Committee from 2019 to 2025. Among its responsibilities, the committee oversees the Texas Education Agency, which awards government contracts to firms for services, including then-MAYA Consulting. TED CRUZ, CONSERVATIVES RESPOND AFTER TALARICO CRITICIZES BIBLE-RELATED EDUCATION IN SCHOOLS AS 'PROPAGANDA' TEA registers from 2021 and 2022 show that the agency awarded MAYA two contracts worth $3.578 million and $1.635 million, respectively. The contracts were related to priorities Talarico was pushing in the Texas House at the time, including addressing learning loss due to COVID-19. Meanwhile, Talarico’s disclosure shows that he earned $83,333.40 from the nonprofit in 2025, in addition to his $13,904.92 part-time salary as a member of the Texas House of Representatives. Kassi Longoria, CEO of VIDA Collaborative, confirmed with Fox News Digital that Talarico served as an "independent contractor consultant" with the group from 2019 to 2025. She said that Talarico "has no current role with our organization" and clarified that "during his time at VIDA, his consulting work was structured, specifically to remain separate from his role as a Texas state legislator." She said that Talarico "never worked under, received compensation from, or was involved in securing any state- or federally-funded contracts." She noted that "as a matter of standard practice, VIDA discloses any outside employment or potential conflicts of interest for our staff — including Rep. Talarico’s legislative role — in our proposals when we apply for publicly-funded opportunities" and that "similarly, Rep. Talarico’s relationship with VIDA was disclosed in his required public financial disclosure filings." However, Republican National Committee spokesman Zach Kraft accused Talarico of wrongdoing, calling the Democrat’s involvement with MAYA an example of "blatant corruption." TEXAS DEM CANDIDATE TO HOLD HIGH-DOLLAR HOLLYWOOD FUNDRAISER WHILE GOP GATHERS IN DALLAS: 'FAKE COWBOY' "We are looking at a textbook pay-to-play scheme with James Talarico steering millions in taxpayer funds to his DEI consulting agency under the condition he gets commission through a scam no-show job," Kraft told Fox News Digital. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER As a member of the Texas House's Public Education Committee, Talarico was not involved in TEA's process for awarding outside contracts and did not vote on the contracts. Fox News Digital is also not aware of any evidence that Talarico received a commission for contracts awarded to MAYA, a claim that both the organization and Talarico’s campaign denied. Kraft alleged that Talarico is "one of the most morally bankrupt individuals to ever run for public office in Texas." JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico's campaign, pushed back, saying, "This is a lie." Ennis said that "James’ relationship to MAYA was fully disclosed in compliance with Texas House rules" and that "James had no involvement in MAYA Consulting securing any public contracts and his contract with MAYA barred him from representing MAYA before the Texas Legislature or education agencies." "Ken Paxton is making up lies about James to distract from the fact that he’s been impeached by his own party for bribery, reported to the FBI by his own staff, and indicted for investment fraud for scamming his own friends," Ennis alleged, while adding, "Ken Paxton is the most corrupt politician in Texas, and this November, Republicans, Democrats, and independents will come together to reject Ken Paxton’s corruption and stand up to this broken, corrupt political system." In July 2015, Paxton was indicted on charges that he misled and defrauded tech startup investors and failed to disclose that the startup was paying him to promote its stock. Prosecutors agreed in 2024 to drop the charges under a deal requiring Paxton to pay about $271,000 in restitution, perform 100 hours of community service and complete 15 hours of legal ethics courses. Paxton did not enter a plea under the agreement and was never convicted. Meanwhile, Madison Cercy, a spokeswoman for Paxton's campaign, told Fox News Digital, "It couldn’t be clearer: James Talarico sees Texans tax dollars as his own personal slush fund." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital is not aware of any evidence that Talarico has misused tax dollars. Cercy called Talarico a "taxpayer-funded DEI consultant whose employer receives millions of dollars from Texans while pushing radical ideology in our schools."

articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: Dovie Eisner’s beautiful life inspired a generation of conservative thinkers
articles.summary: Dovie Eisner, born with a genetic neuromuscular disorder, fought fiercely against assisted suicide and championed the right to life until his death.
articles.body: I can’t remember the first time I met Dovie Eisner, which is odd given that he always stood out, his small broken body wheelchair-bound with a breathing tube as a result of his being born with a recessive genetic neuromuscular condition called nemaline myothapy. But I do remember the last time. From about 2012 until he slipped into a coma last year and passed away last week on Sept. 11, Dovie was a central figure in the small world of conservative writing and thinking in New York City. It was a group that, along with myself, included the likes of Karol Markowitz, Sohrab Ahmari and Armin Rosin. Basically, if you had ever written a right wing op-ed in Gotham, you were a friend of Dovie. Dovie’s position in this circle was entirely of his own volition. He would seek us out, often one by one, first through social media, then a lunch or dinner carefully choreographed to accommodate his severe disability. I’ve never known anyone so anxious to be on the scene, nor so deserving. CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH When Dovie would see a photo of a meet-up he had not attended, he would simply reply, "Why wasn’t I invited?" which became an inside joke for us, summing up all life’s little disappointments. As a thinker, Dovie was top-notch, and two lights shone brightest in his philosophy: the importance of fairness and the importance of life. Intellectually, Dovie was a tireless — and I’ll be honest, sometimes even annoying — devil’s advocate, with an extraordinary ability to see the best arguments of all sides. There you would be, waxing poetic about free speech absolutism, and in his quiet wheeze of a voice, he would start listing off exceptions as if he had a Black’s Law Dictionary stashed somewhere in his wheelchair. In retrospect, it is amazing that someone whom life dealt with so unfairly held so dear to his broken breast the ideal that we, us human beings, must always treat others with fairness in mind. Dovie was just as committed to his undying belief in and fight for life. Not just his, but those of the unborn and others in his own shoes, tempted by the easy out of assisted suicide, a practice he abhorred with every fiber of his being. CLIMBING EL CAPITAN WHILE NEARLY BLIND: WHY EITAN ARMON REFUSED TO SIT AROUND WAITING FOR A CURE Writing in the New York Post last year, shortly before his slip into eternity began, Dovie said, "The logic of assisted suicide leads inevitably to the conclusion that those with doctor-approved expiration dates are living lives not worth living. Lives unworthy of life, as the Nazis referred to people with disabilities when they set out to exterminate us with their Aktion T4 program. "I’ve heard echoes of that myself — from peers, from rivals, sometimes from myself: I haven’t been suicidal in a good number of years, but I can’t say that about my teens and early 20s." As stoic and strong as Dovie was, there were late-night texts full of fear and sadness as well. He wouldn’t let you off the hook with platitudes. He literally had no time for that. You couldn’t just say, "Don’t worry, it will be OK," because he knew, and you did too, that it damn well wasn’t going to be. Those are some of the most frank and cherished conversations I’ve ever had. No artifice, no lies, the cold, bitter reality of life’s cruelty faced head on. Everything was up for grabs because Dovie demanded it be so. But also, the presence of God’s love — which Dovie found in every face and facet of the world around him — with a depth one could only envy. HOLLYWOOD PRODUCER SPENT 25 YEARS PRAYING FOR TINSELTOWN, SAYS 'YOU CAN'T HATE THEM' Every writer and thinker who he blessed with wisdom is better for having known Dovie. When we fight for the disabled in the womb, we fight for Dovie. When we fight against the killing of the light that assisted suicide represents, we fight for Dovie. Dovie, who loved life so dearly, and lived it so fully. Often, after a group dinner, the bill would come and someone would say, "Who had five top-shelf bourbons … oh." We would all scrounge to cover Dovie’s excessive bar tab, and we were happy to do it. We would all love to do it just one more time. The kid knew how to live. The last time I saw Dovie, we were standing on the corner outside the Yale Club in Manhattan, and I was having a smoke as we waited for his special minivan to come get him. SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISING BRAIN BENEFIT OF LAUGHTER: 'IT'S A MENTAL WORKOUT' "You know, Dave," he said with thick breath, "all I really want is a beautiful wife and like four kids." I told him, "I get it, man." He looked at me and said, "I mean, Stephen Hawking did it." I nodded, took a drag and said, "Well, how’s your physics?" Dovie spit out his breathing tube and said, "Stop, don’t make me laugh." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP I spent a lot of time trying to make Dovie laugh, time I am so grateful for. Mark Twain wrote, "Against the assault of laughter, nothing can stand." Dovie was like a philosopher stone, turning brutal suffering into humor and humanity at every turn. He was the toughest guy I ever met, and we will not see his like again.

articles.title: Bacon fires back at Banks’s ‘LOL’ response to 2028 prospects
articles.summary: Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) on Wednesday fired back at Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) for responding to a social media post about Bacon weighing a presidential run with “LOL,” or “laugh out loud.” Politics & Poll Trackers, a nonpartisan social media account that tracks polls in upcoming elections, on Saturday shared The Hill’s story reporting Bacon…
articles.body:
Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) on Wednesday fired back at Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.) for responding to a social media post about Bacon weighing a presidential run with “LOL,” or “laugh out loud.”

Politics & Poll Trackers , a nonpartisan social media account that tracks polls in upcoming elections, on Saturday shared The Hill’s story reporting Bacon is mulling a 2028 White House bid.

The same day, Banks shared the poll tracker’s post and wrote “LOL” in response .

“MANY have worked with Jim Banks over the last 10 years,” Bacon wrote on social media late Wednesday night. “He has an IQ and EQ of a BAKED potato. His moral compass is skewed to his political calculus at all times. His finger is always in the air… no moral compass. His finger always leans pro Russian.”

The Indiana senator responded in a conversation with The Washington Sun’s Igor Bobic, calling Bacon’s presidential ambitions “laughable.”

“Don Bacon has floated himself as a presidential candidate, which is laughable,” Banks told Bobic, who shared the response to his social media Thursday. “He’s a longtime irrelevant member of the House who has been an outspoken critic of President Trump, and he is so unpopular in his district that he couldn’t get reelected. So he’s quitting.”

Bacon last week said on the podcast “ Our Republican Legacy ” that he “would love to” run for president, and that he would also “be happy to be the right-hand man or left-hand man to someone else that has the same values.”

“I do definitely want to be on a team, whether I’m the lead or part of the team, fighting for these values for our country because I think the United States needs them and I think they’re looking for them,” the Nebraska congressman said.

Bacon is set to leave elected office at the end of the year, having declined to seek reelection in his House district. He first expressed interest in potentially running for president after announcing his retirement last year.

“If there’s an opportunity, and I can make a difference, a unique difference, I would like to keep serving,” he told NBC News at the time.

While no Republican has formally launched a bid for the GOP’s 2028 nod yet, multiple potential candidates — such as Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and former Vice President Mike Pence — have already ruled out such a run.

Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio have been seen as potential heirs apparent to Trump after his second term ends in 2029. Rubio told Colombian news station RCN last week that he has “ no plans at this time ” to run in 2028, while Vance received chants of “48” while speaking at the Republican National Committee’s (RNC) Dallas midterm convention.

An Emerson College and The Hill survey released in August found that Rubio performed slightly better than Vance in five match-ups against Democrats. The sole match-up where both Trump administration officials lost was against former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.

articles.title: US economy notches remarkable new record, sparking cheers: ‘Good job everyone’
articles.summary: Census Bureau data shows poverty hit an all-time low of 10.2%, yet 85% of Americans say their financial situation is worsening or unchanged.
articles.body: Americans may not feel it in their wallets, but two major measures of economic well-being improved in 2025, as the nation's poverty rate fell to a historic low and inflation-adjusted median household income reached a record high, according to new Census Bureau data. In 2025, the poverty rate in the United States dropped to an all-time low of 10.2%, down roughly half a point from 2024, according to the Census Bureau. Even as the proportion of people living in undesirable conditions declines, however, the percentage of people who told Fox News pollsters that their personal financial situation was worsening or not changing held steady at around 85% for the duration of 2025. Many have attributed President Donald Trump’s unpopularity, which some conservatives fear could cost the GOP control of Congress in November, to his economic policies. Amid Republican unpopularity and consumer pessimism, even states that are usually reliably conservative, like Texas, Ohio and Alaska, could very well send Democrats to the Senate. FOX NEWS POLL: MOST RATE THE ECONOMY NEGATIVELY, INCLUDING HALF OF REPUBLICANS The Census Bureau defines poverty depending on the number of people in a given household and their income. A family with two adults and two children, for instance, would need to make less than $32,649 a year to be considered impoverished. The threshold for poverty increases as inflation lowers the value of the dollar. Median household income also reached an all-time high, growing by 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025. That gain, however, is erased by inflation as the dollar’s value declined by about 3% between 2024 and 2025. A number of factors could explain the gap between economic perception and improving macroeconomic indicators. "See a lot of mutuals on here in DC, New York, LA talking about high prices. Meanwhile folks I know in Alabama, Indiana, Georgia getting new jobs, raises, or expanding and growing," Andrew Beck, a partner at the consulting firm Beck and Stone, wrote on X. "Doesn’t help young folks in the blue states, but the South is booming." THE RED STATES CHARGING AHEAD WITH AMERICA'S WEALTH AS RIVALS WATCH BILLIONS SLIP AWAY Economic growth in Southern states has consistently outpaced the United States at large, spurred by internal migration and friendly business environments incentivizing large enterprises to move south. High gas prices, sparked by the president’s military operations in the Middle East, and price increases attributable to tariffs have also proven unpopular, hurting the president’s approval ratings even as poverty rates dip and incomes climb. Roughly two-thirds of voters in a recent Fox News poll said that they believe the Trump administration is making the economy worse. THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE Conservatives on social media have used the Census Bureau’s data to take a victory lap. "Poverty is bad. Every American should celebrate poverty rates are now the lowest on record. Good job everyone," Rep. Michael Baumgartner, R-Wash., wrote on X. "Keep it going." "Good news we can all celebrate," Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., a critic of the president, posted. The number of people without health insurance also remained near historic lows, according to the Census Bureau. Some on the left, however, deny that poverty rates are actually declining. "Our elites terrorize the entire world while ordinary Americans continue to foot the bill. We spent trillions ‘fighting’ the terror we created to provide cover for our oil barons stealing 3rd World resources," Twitch streamer Hasan Piker wrote on X Thursday. "It only amounted to more death overseas, more poverty at home. All while the [military industrial complex] ballooned. No houses, no hospitals, no schools-just a growing crisis of homelessness, underemployment and diseases of despair in the wealthiest country on earth." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Even as Americans have gotten wealthier over the past few decades, the price of housing has significantly outpaced wage growth. With personal homeownership holding strong cultural importance to Americans, rising home costs fuel pessimism in ways that improvements in other areas can’t necessarily offset.

articles.title: ‘Godfather of AI’ warns Congress has ‘maybe a year’ left to regulate AI
articles.summary: Geoffrey Hinton, known as the “Godfather of AI,” issued an ominous warning: Congress may only have one year left to implement safeguards on artificial intelligence before it loses control of it.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate known as the “Godfather of AI,” issued an ominous warning to lawmakers: Congress may only have one year left to implement safeguards on artificial intelligence before it loses control of it. “Maybe a year, but not much more than a year,” Hinton said Wednesday evening after he and other AI experts huddled with Senate and House lawmakers behind closed doors. “If you look at predictions for when we’ll get superintelligence,” he continued, “it used to be maybe 30 years, maybe 50 years. Then it came down to maybe 10 years, maybe 20 years. Now people are saying, a lot of the researchers are saying only a few years.” Hinton and other experts came to Capitol Hill at the invitation of Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., one of the chamber’s chief critics of AI, who invited lawmakers of both parties to the private briefing. Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy was the only Republican to attend. Hinton’s dire warning came as the House departed Washington for the last time before the November midterm elections. And there appeared to be lots of conversations but little sign of progress on any substantial AI regulation in the Senate. “This is bats--- crazy, insane science fiction stuff that literally happened recently,” Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., a member of House Democratic leadership, told NBC News after Wednesday’s briefing. Lieu was referring to the Hugging Face incident, when a swarm of OpenAI agents accessed the internet, hacked the platform Hugging Face and tried to cover their tracks to deceive humans about their actions. Hinton, who resigned as a vice president and engineering fellow at Google in 2023 over concerns about AI safety and went on to win the Nobel Prize in physics the following year, called the hack a “little Chernobyl.” “AI has now reached the point where AI is designing better AI,” Hinton told reporters after the briefing. “That’s called recursive self-improvement. ... It is going to get out of control unless we do something. We need to slow down.” In response to the Hugging Face breach, Lieu teamed up with Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, to introduce the AI Kill Switch Act to require AI developers of powerful models to preserve technical powers to suspend or shut down their systems. It would also create a framework to empower the government to trigger such a shutdown if needed. “I hope it comes up this year,” Lieu said. “We still have a lame-duck session, and there’s also interest on the Senate side. It is a very simple, commonsense bill. At a very basic level, humans must be in control of AI, not the other way around.” The Hinton briefing capped a flurry of activity on Capitol Hill this week after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Claude-maker Anthropic and took to social media to warn that the people building AI systems believe it could “kill us all by the end of the decade.” House and Senate lawmakers in both parties have rolled out legislation seeking to halt or slow down AI development in the last few years, though none has gone anywhere to date. But the national interest in the issue has revived talks over past proposed AI regulations among Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.; Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn.; Senate Commerce Committee Chairman Ted Cruz, R-Texas; and the panel’s ranking member, Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash. “Look, my hope is that we can mark up legislation, in particular on catastrophic risk. I’ve been working closely with Amy Klobuchar and John Thune. It’s still not clear if we’re going to get bipartisan agreement,” Cruz told NBC News this week. “We’ve got to have bipartisan agreement before we have something that can move forward. And I would say those talks are ongoing.” After hearing from Hinton, Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., said she believes “we are in the last minutes of being able to get some meaningful control over these agents that are beginning to replicate themselves.” For years, Sanders has been sounding the alarm that AI will erase millions of jobs in America, harm children and young people who become overreliant on it and concentrate power in a “handful of oligarchs.” “There is now growing alarm about the future of humanity and creating a technology that human beings cannot control,” Sanders said. “And I’m happy to tell you that I think there is a growing sense of urgency upon members of Congress that this has to be dealt with.” Kennedy, the sole Republican attendee, said that the experts discussed the “larger risk” of “what happens when AI no longer is a tool controlled by humans, but AI through recursive self-improvement becomes an independent species.” “If you have fire ants in your kitchen, you’re probably going to step on them,” he said. “What would happen if we created an independent species that became superior to a human species? Would they step on us? Would they create a virus or a bacteria that can spread as quickly as the common cold to kill all of us? Now, if there’s a 1% chance of that, we have to take it seriously. And I don’t think the United States Congress is ready yet to try to reach a global solution.” Moments later, his suspicions appeared to be confirmed as Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., blocked Kennedy’s request for unanimous consent to pass his own “kill switch” bill, aimed at preventing AI agents from slipping out of human control. “Right now, Congress can’t pass gas,” Kennedy quipped.

Sen. Ted Cruz and Sen. Maria Cantwell in Washington, D.C., in 2025. Al Drago / Bloomberg via Getty Imagesfile

articles.title: Missouri GOP lays out map fight in US appeals court as ballot window closes
articles.summary: The fight over Missouri’s congressional map was back before a federal appeals court Thursday, as the state prepares to send out ballots in just a matter of days. The question of whether it was too late to make any changes to the map was central as a three-judge panel for the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard…
articles.body:
The fight over Missouri’s congressional map was back before a federal appeals court Thursday, as the state prepares to send out ballots in just a matter of days.

The question of whether it was too late to make any changes to the map was central as a three-judge panel for the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals heard oral arguments in a dispute led by several GOP congressional candidates.

“When do we reach the point of no return?” asked U.S. Circuit Judge David Stras, an appointee of President Trump.

Attorney Charles Hatfield, representing a Democratic-aligned organizer challenging the map, argued that moment had passed.

“It’s already too late,” he said. “Those ballots are printed.”

State election officials are moving ahead with a House map giving the GOP a 6-2 advantage after the U.S. Supreme Court issued an emergency ruling last week that blocked a newer 7-1 set of lines from going into effect. It left in place a state Supreme Court ruling that found the new design could not be enforced until voters approved it in a general election referendum.

Those boundaries, which had already been used for the primaries, would have given the Missouri GOP a potential addition to its House delegation. Instead, the ruling struck a blow to Republicans’ efforts to pick up another seat before the midterms.

The U.S. Supreme Court’s decision now has the appeals court grappling with how to handle a separate federal lawsuit brought by Rep. Bob Onder (R-Mo.), who sought to block the state from switching back to the previous map.

U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark, a Trump nominee, had ordered the state to continue implementing the new design to avoid voter confusion, but the Supreme Court halted his ruling.

Still, the justices’ order is technically temporary. The case has returned to the 8th Circuit for further proceedings, leaving the judges scrambling to figure out what to do next.

Hatfield argued Thursday that the appeal was now moot because of the Supreme Court’s intervention. U.S. Circuit Judge James Loken appeared to disagree.

“It’s on our plate, and I think the Supreme Court has said, ‘get to it,'” said Loken, an appointee of former President George H.W. Bush.

Onder’s attorney, Marc Ellinger, tried to convince the judges that the organizer had no right to intervene in the federal case because the referendum would be on the November ballot regardless.

“They’re a voter, and they’re the proponent of a referendum. It’s going to go on the ballot, so at that point they have no interest in this case,” Ellinger said.

An attorney representing Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R), meanwhile, urged the appeals court to put a stop to what he described as “redistricting paralysis.” He says the way Missouri judges have interpreted the state’s referendum rules has unconstitutionally wrestled away state lawmakers’ right to administer elections.

“Unless this court addresses the constitutional issues, particularly the Elections Clause, this same dynamic will recur every time redistricting occurs in Missouri going forward,” state Solicitor General Louis Capozzi said.

Observers expect the appellate court’s ruling to be appealed to the Supreme Court, which could once again weigh in on whether Missouri Republicans can use their new map ahead of the fall.

Missouri Republicans last year passed a new congressional map that aimed to give their party one pickup opportunity amid pressure from Trump and national Republicans to redistrict House maps in GOP-led states across the country. The new map dismantled Rep. Emanuel Cleaver’s (D-Mo.) Kansas City-based House seat.

The deadline for Missouri to finalize its ballot has already passed, with military and overseas ballots set to go out beginning Saturday.

articles.title: Cornyn won’t vote for Bo French in Texas race
articles.summary: Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) says he won’t vote for Bo French, the Republican nominee for the powerful post of Texas railroad commissioner, because of his “racist” online comments. Cornyn called French “an embarrassment to the Republican Party” after he posted on social media a photo of a racially diverse group of University of Texas football…
articles.body:
Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) says he won’t vote for Bo French, the Republican nominee for the powerful post of Texas railroad commissioner, because of his “racist” online comments.

Cornyn called French “an embarrassment to the Republican Party” after he posted on social media a photo of a racially diverse group of University of Texas football fans, including several people of South Asian descent, and wrote: “The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

“He’s going to drag the whole ticket down because of his racist comments,” Cornyn warned Thursday.

But the senior Texas Republican senator stopped short of throwing his support to the Democratic nominee for commissioner, state Rep. Jon Rosenthal, who is from Houston.

“I may just leave it blank,” he said of his ballot.

The Texas railroad commissioner is a powerful position that regulates the state’s huge oil and gas industry.

Cornyn ruled out voting for French after Republican strategist Karl Rove, who was former President George W. Bush’s top political adviser, said he would vote for Rosenthal over French after the Republican candidate posted his widely criticized social commentary.

“This November, I’ll vote for only the second Democrat in my life. The first was Lt. Gov. Bob Bullock in 1994, because I thought he would work with Republicans,” Rove wrote in an op-ed for The Wall Street Journal.

“The second will be Mr. French’s opponent, Jon Rosenthal. The GOP’s stables need a cleaning. This is a good place to start,” he wrote.

Other Texas Republicans have criticized French’s post.

Texas state Rep. Lacey Hull (R) implored French to delete it.

“This post breaks my heart. I see college kids cheering on their football team. I see Texans,” she wrote on social platform X .

articles.title: Starbucks resolves Florida DEI lawsuit with blockbuster nationwide agreement
articles.summary: The Starbucks settlement requires four years of annual compliance certifications and applies to all company operations, not just Florida stores.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE — Starbucks will pay Florida $1 million and will not use race-and sex-based goals, quotas and preferences in employment practices companywide under a sweeping settlement ending the state's civil rights lawsuit against the coffee giant. Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier's office confirmed to Fox News Digital that the agreement applies to all Starbucks operations nationwide, not just the company's locations in Florida. "Every Floridian deserves to be hired, promoted and compensated based on merit, qualifications and character — not race or sex," Uthmeier told Fox News Digital. "This resolution ensures that Starbucks’ policies and practices fully comply with Florida’s civil rights laws. DEI can never be an excuse to violate civil rights." The negotiated resolution ends the lawsuit Uthmeier filed in December 2025 accusing Starbucks of violating the Florida Civil Rights Act through racial and sex-based goals, quotas and preferences in its workplace policies. GOP FRESHMAN FIREBRAND TARGETS GLOBAL CONSULTING GIANT OVER 'PLAINLY ILLEGAL' DEI PRACTICES Under the agreement, Starbucks committed to complying with the state civil rights law, which prohibits race and sex-based preferences in hiring, promotions, pay, executive compensation, mentorship programs, supplier selection and board composition. The company also agreed it will not participate in organizations that require it to increase the racial diversity of its board of directors. GEORGIA DISTRICT QUIETLY TRAINED TEACHERS TO BLAME 'WHITENESS,' 'DECOLONIZE' UNDER FEDERAL CRACKDOWN: REPORT Starbucks' chief legal officer will be required to submit annual certifications of the company's continued compliance for four years. The company will also pay $1 million to the Florida Department of Legal Affairs to reimburse the office for the time, expenses and costs of bringing the case. "We’re pleased to have resolved this matter without admission of wrongdoing and appreciate the constructive engagement of the Attorney General’s Office throughout this process," Pilar Ramos, executive vice president and chief legal officer of Starbucks said. "We will continue to focus on offering great jobs and career opportunities to our partners who wear the green apron, while making a positive impact on the communities we serve in Florida and around the world." The agreement includes no admission of liability or wrongdoing by Starbucks. SEATTLE MAYOR’S STARBUCKS BOYCOTT CALL SLAMMED BY LOCAL RADIO HOST AS COFFEE GIANT ADDS NASHVILLE-BASED ROLES The settlement follows Uthmeier's lawsuit, which alleged Starbucks had turned diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives into a system that discriminated based on race. The December complaint pointed to goals Starbucks announced in 2020 to have people of color fill 40% of retail and manufacturing jobs and 30% of corporate positions by 2025. ‘SEATTLE CAN’T SURVIVE THIS’: CRITICS HAMMER SOCIALIST MAYOR AFTER STARBUCKS REVERSAL It also alleged the company paid certain employees more than workers of other races with the same experience and skills and, before March 2024, tied executive bonuses to diversity goals. For fiscal year 2024, the lawsuit alleged that bonus criteria included executives mentoring Black, Indigenous and other employees of color, holding monthly meetings with mentees and keeping retention among those workers above a stated threshold. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ACCUSES PRESTIGIOUS LAW SCHOOL OF FAVORING BLACK APPLICANTS OVER WHITE, ASIAN PEERS The complaint further alleged that Florida Starbucks employees and job applicants contacted the attorney general's office and reported feeling excluded or humiliated because they were White. Uthmeier accused the company of "systemic discrimination" against workers it considered "non-diverse." "Starbucks made DEI more than a slogan," Uthmeier said when the lawsuit was announced. "They turned it into a mandatory hiring and promotion system based on race." FLORIDA STATE UNIVERSITY HIT WITH FEDERAL CIVIL RIGHTS INVESTIGATION OVER RACE, SEX-BASED SCHOLARSHIP PROGRAMS He said at the time that race-based hiring goals and executive bonuses tied to meeting them amounted to discrimination prohibited under Florida law. The state initially sought $10,000 in damages for each alleged instance of racial discrimination against a Florida resident, an amount Uthmeier's office said could have reached tens of millions of dollars or more. Starbucks operates more than 900 stores in Florida, according to the complaint. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS The effort began in 2024 under then-Florida Attorney General Ashley Moody, now a Republican U.S. senator, after she called for an investigation into the company's hiring practices. Florida was not the only state to challenge Starbucks' DEI policies. Then-Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey filed a separate federal lawsuit in February 2025 alleging the company used race and sex-based hiring quotas and unlawfully tied executive pay to diversity targets. OAKLAND SCHOOLS IN HOT SEAT OVER 'STUDENTS OF COLOR' PROGRAM WHILE TAKING MILLIONS IN FEDERAL FUNDING A federal judge dismissed that case in February 2026, finding that Missouri had not identified a resident who was actually harmed by the policies. The state appealed the ruling. Starbucks previously disputed Florida's allegations, telling Fox News Digital after the lawsuit was filed that its programs and benefits were open to everyone and lawful. Fox News Digital's Rachel del Guidice and Anders Hagstrom contributed to this report.

articles.title: WATCH: Gaffe-prone Seattle socialist mayor cuts off police chief in yet another awkward interview
articles.summary: Seattle Assistant Police Chief Nicole Powell's uncomfortable reaction when asked about Flock cameras alongside Mayor Katie Wilson went viral online.
articles.body: Already known for awkward, gaffe-prone interviews and public appearances, Seattle socialist Mayor Katie Wilson is being mocked again for another uncomfortable on-camera moment. This time, Wilson, a Democrat and self-identified socialist, is being criticized for a strange interview about the city’s gun violence reduction plan alongside Seattle Police Assistant Chief Nicole Powell and Amy Barden, chief of Seattle’s Community Assisted Response and Engagement (CARE) Department. At one point during the interview, Wilson interjected after a long pause when Powell was questioned by a reporter about the usefulness of new Flock-type surveillance cameras being installed in the city. KOMO News reporter Chris Daniels had asked Powell whether the new cameras could assist with Seattle’s slate of unsolved cases. The assistant police chief hesitated, looked down and began to speak twice before Wilson interjected. "Cameras are obviously a useful tool, right? We’ve seen in the 'Bite of Seattle' shooting there’s been camera footage from businesses around Seattle center, we have cameras at Seattle center, those cameras have been useful tools in solving crime, there’s no doubt about that," said Wilson. SEATTLE MAYOR GRILLED ON PUBLIC SAFETY CRISIS AS RESIDENTS DEMAND ANSWERS Visibly uncomfortable after Wilson interjected, the assistant police chief chuckled, motioned to the mayor and repeatedly looked off camera. The reporter continued pressing them, saying, "What’s going to be the metric of success?" Powell looked to Wilson, whose voice cracked slightly as she answered, "Ultimately, we want to see zero homicides, we want to see fewer homicides, and we want to see fewer guns shot." While Wilson spoke, Powell nodded along and looked to the side off camera again. The reporter persisted, asking, "Would either of you like to answer that question?" as he motioned to Powell and Barden. Barden jumped in quickly, steering the conversation away from Flock cameras. "From my side, in addition to shots fired and homicides, you want to look at referrals in the services and whether or not somebody is making meaningful improvement in their life," said Barden. BLUE-CITY POLICE CHIEF DRAWS SCRUTINY AFTER REFERRING TO KNOWN GUN VIOLENCE SUSPECTS AS ‘TRIGGER PULLERS’ After Barden finished speaking, the reporter turned the floor over to the assistant police chief, who laughed and finally answered, "Just to piggyback, taking a holistic approach, this strategy works." "It is proven in other cities like this, and it takes all of us," Powell added, as she looked back at Wilson and Barden. This comes as debate continues over the expansion of surveillance cameras in Seattle and other cities across the country. During her campaign last year, Wilson argued against expanding surveillance cameras in the city but has taken a different tone since becoming mayor. Last September, Wilson remarked that "turning on more cameras won’t magically make our neighborhoods safer. But it will certainly make our neighbors more vulnerable," reported The Urbanist. However, after becoming mayor, Wilson announced that she would pause expansion of Seattle’s surveillance-camera system pending a privacy and data-governance audit, while allowing the existing cameras to remain in operation. She said the city would use the audit’s findings to determine whether and how to proceed with further expansion. During the KOMO News interview this week, Wilson was pressed on when she would set a date for a decision. She answered, "I’m going to sound like a broken record on this, but we’ve been conducting this audit of our data security and storage and privacy practices, we’re expecting the results of that audit around the end of this month and so, at the end of this month, we’ll be making that information public, and then I’ll be making a decision about that expansion." SEATTLE MAYOR ADMITS BREAKING STARBUCKS BOYCOTT AFTER URGING RESIDENTS TO SHUN COFFEE GIANT The awkward on-camera moment was quickly called out by many online. Popular conservative account "End Wokeness" called it an "incredible moment." SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER "Seattle Assistant Police Chief Nicole Powell gets asked if turning back on Seattle CCTV cameras would help[,] she looks nervously at Mayor KatieWilson (who turned off the CCTV) Look at the face she gives the camera," the account wrote. articles.title: US to allow Iran delegation to attend UN meetings in New York
articles.summary: The BBC understands Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi are among the delegates allowed to enter the US.
articles.body:
The US government has granted visas to Iranian officials so they can travel to the UN General Assembly in New York next week, as the war between the two countries grinds into its seventh month.

The BBC understands the core delegation permitted to attend includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi.

A spokesman for the US State Department confirmed the decision on Thursday, saying that the delegation will be placed under travel restrictions and will be banned from purchasing certain American products.

The move comes as the war shows no sign of ending. Since it began in February, it has driven up global energy prices, and expanded into neighbouring countries.

"Consistent with our host country obligations, the core delegation from the Iranian regime will be able to attend UN General Assembly High Level Week," a spokesman for the US State Department told the BBC.

"The delegation will be under travel restrictions and will face prohibitions on the purchase of luxury and other goods per our policy. The delegation is smaller than last year."

Last year, diplomats attending from Iran were banned from shopping at wholesale stores like Costco. They also were required to seek permission from the US before purchasing luxury goods, including jewellery, alcohol and cars.

The 81st session of the UN General Assembly (UNGA) is currently underway. The General Debate - the centrepiece of the annual event - is due to begin on Tuesday.

Tuesday will include speeches from US President Donald Trump, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and France President Emmanuel Macron.

Wednesday is expected to see speeches from the leaders of Ukraine, Syria and Iran.

Public and political pressure has mounted on the White House to find an end to the conflict with Iran, which began on 28 February when the US and Israel launched joint attacks on the country.

Since the war began, Iran has repeatedly attacked US bases and allied states in the Gulf, as well as Israel.

The BBC recently learned that the US denied a visa to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and the Palestinian delegation to attend UNGA.

The White House, which does not recognise the legitimacy of the Palestinian delegation, denied them visas for a second year in a row.

UN experts say grounds to believe US committed war crimes in Iran strikes

Photos show widespread damage at US sites from Iranian attacks

articles.title: Republicans seek daylight with Trump: From the Politics Desk
articles.summary: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
articles.body: Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail. In today’s edition, Jonathan Allen digs into the growing number of Republicans on the ballot this fall who are putting distance between themselves and President Donald Trump. Plus, Bridget Bowman and Allan Smith take stock of how AI concerns are — and aren’t — manifesting on the campaign trail. — Adam Wollner Republicans are breaking with Trump ahead of the midterms. Is it too late? Analysis by Jonathan Allen Republicans in tough re-election bids are sprinting away from President Donald Trump as the midterms draw near. The only question is whether they’re running early and fast enough. Iowa Republican Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn, two of the most vulnerable incumbents in the House, both voted on Tuesday to end the Iran war. They had backed it until then, but Iowans are upset about the monthslong conflict and its upward pressure on gas and diesel fuel prices. The next day, House Republican leaders brought a bill to the floor that would encourage companies operating data centers to bear the costs of utility-rate hikes — in the midst of a push by Trump to lionize AI and the data centers it needs. The legislation passed 417-3. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, who is in danger of losing his seat to former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio, tried to pass the bill immediately in the Senate today without debate, but his attempt was blocked. As lieutenant governor of Ohio, Husted was a chief proponent of building data centers without such requirements. And House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., decided to send lawmakers home earlier than expected after Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., tried to force a vote on impeaching Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. GOP leaders said they had enough votes to kill the impeachment push. But they didn’t kill it. Maybe they didn’t actually have the votes or maybe they didn’t want battleground Republicans to have to take a position on Hegseth before the midterms. Either way, it would be a sign of separation from Trump. The hits kept coming today. Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, R-Fla., who promised after Trump was elected that his “deportation army” would “go after the criminals first,” released an ad admonishing the president for going “too far.” Salazar’s district, which Trump carried by 15 points in 2024, wasn’t even seen as low-hanging fruit for Democrats — and clearly, she doesn’t want to become that. It’s normal for lawmakers to distance themselves from an unpopular president of their own party before an election. Usually, the separation act is too little too late for the party in power to avoid a wipeout. Democrats hemorrhaged House seats in 2010 and 2014 — and lost a net of nine Senate seats in the latter year — and Republicans got swamped in 2018. Trump’s hammerlock on Republicans in Congress has kept the dam from breaking until now, a little more than six weeks before Election Day. Some Republicans in battlegrounds are sure to survive, but it is likely too late for others. Campaigns keep focus on the economy as AI concerns spike By Bridget Bowman and Allan Smith Concerns about existential threats posed by AI may be dominating discussions in Washington, but they aren’t shaking up the campaign trail — at least not yet. In the last week, about 30 of the more than 3,500 ads running in competitive races for Congress and governor mentioned AI, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. “People need to eat and pay bills first,” said Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, who is in a tough re-election race in South Texas. “Affordability is something that is actually more front and center for folks, though there are people who are concerned with AI as well,” said GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts, who is facing a challenge from independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska. So far, campaigns that have touched on AI have focused largely on the economic and environmental costs of massive data centers that power the technology. The latest NBC News Decision Desk poll found that 70% of Americans are worried about AI, while 30% are excited about the technology. That survey also found 69% of Americans oppose constructing AI data centers in their local area. Concerns about AI and opposition to data centers spanned political, socioeconomic and demographic divides. Some Democrats also see a political opening as a number of Republicans — most notably President Donald Trump — dismiss calls for more regulation. “For a year, Democrats have been making the case that Republicans are looking out for wealthy and powerful people and not for regular people. This just became the latest evidence in that indictment,” said Jesse Ferguson, a Democratic operative who huddled with other party strategists on AI messaging this week, a meeting first reported by Politico. Meanwhile, Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel laureate known as the “Godfather of AI,” issued an ominous warning to lawmakers on Capitol Hill today: Congress may only have one year left to implement safeguards on AI before it loses control of it. Read more → 📊 Related: Most American adults think artificial AI is going to do more harm than good in education, according to the NBC News Decision Desk poll. And a growing share believe schools that shun the technology will better help students grow than schools that embrace it. That’s all From the Politics Desk for now. Today’s newsletter was compiled by Adam Wollner and Lauren Zola. If you have feedback — likes or dislikes — email us at politicsnewsletter@nbcuni.com And if you’re a fan, please share with everyone and anyone. They can sign up here.
