articles.title: Trump administration gets green light to proceed with homelessness program overhaul
articles.summary: A U.S. appeals court in Boston on Wednesday gave the Trump administration the green light to go forward with a massive overhaul of a homelessness program and its criteria for aid funding. The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals’ three-judge panel halted a Rhode Island-based federal judge’s ruling in March that the changes to the…
articles.body:
A U.S. appeals court in Boston on Wednesday gave the Trump administration the green light to go forward with a massive overhaul of a homelessness program and its criteria for aid funding.

The 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals’ three-judge panel halted a Rhode Island-based federal judge’s ruling in March that the changes to the Continuum of Care (CoC) program were unlawful.

“After careful review of the parties’ briefs and supplemental submissions, we conclude that HUD [Department of Housing and Urban Development] has met its burden to show its entitlement to a stay pending appeal,” the panel wrote in its order. “HUD has made a strong showing that it is likely to succeed on the merits of its challenge to the district court’s holding that the set-aside in the NOFO [Notice of Funding Opportunity] was subject to notice and comment requirements …”

HUD sought to change the rules for receiving $75 million to build housing for homeless families and individuals, and set $1.3 billion aside for transitional housing and supportive services.

The program’s funding goes to states, local governments, tribal governments and nonprofit organizations working to rehouse homeless people and families, individuals fleeing violent situations and others in need of assistance, which it has done since 1987. Congress codified the program in 2009.

“This is a step in the right direction to deliver real and lasting results that serve our most vulnerable — not a failed ideology and those who profit from it,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner wrote on social media Wednesday night.

The Hill reached out to one of the plaintiffs, the National Alliance to End Homelessness, for comment.

The plaintiffs jointly told Reuters that they would evaluate any possible next steps.

“Despite our ​coalition’s repeated triumphs in the lower court, today’s decision will give new life to HUD’s attempt to radically upend this critical program by defunding permanent housing solutions, which ​threatens to push 100,000 Americans into homelessness,” the plaintiffs said.

The Trump administration has criticized the housing-first approach of the program, the outlet reported. U.S. District Judge Mary McElroy, nominated by President Trump, previously blocked the administration from making those changes earlier this year and last year.

Democratic officials in 20 states and Washington, D.C., and homelessness and housing advocacy groups filed lawsuits challenging HUD’s plan, claiming that the changes to CoC threw it into “chaos.”

“Instead of helping us tackle our housing crisis, the Trump administration is once again standing in our way and putting thousands of vulnerable people at risk,” Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell (D) said in a statement when states sued the administration earlier this year.

articles.title: Trump’s transactional presidency takes a more brazen turn
articles.summary: Few things have defined President Donald Trump’s second term as much as his transactionalism. He’s gone to great lengths to wield potential official actions...
articles.body:
Few things have defined President Donald Trump's second term as much as his transactionalism. He's gone to great lengths to wield potential official actions for political and even personal gain in ways simply not seen since at least Watergate.

It's this same sensibility that led to Trump's first impeachment in 2019, after he suggestively tied Ukraine's military aid to that country investigating the Bidens ahead of the 2020 election.

But while that and many of Trump's transactions have relied on implied threats or quid pro quos, he's increasingly coming out and saying them out loud.

His brazenness was on display on multiple fronts over the last eight days. Last week, he promised American adults thousands of dollars each if they elect Republican majorities in November. This week, he's repeatedly threatened to abandon or even tear down the Kennedy Center if he's not allowed to put his name on it.

And on Wednesday night, he jokingly threatened to withhold disaster aid from North Carolina if it elects a Democratic senator (except maybe it's not a joke, judging by Trump's track record).

To so openly talk about tying official actions to his political and personal interest should be scandalous. And it was a scandal in Trump's first term, as evidenced by his impeachment.

His transactionalism is treated as less scandalous today in large part because Americans already know it's how Trump's been conducting business for the last 20 months.

But it shouldn't be lost just how brazen it is now.

Trump's joke that might not be a joke about North Carolina disaster aid

At a Wednesday night rally, Trump tied North Carolina getting disaster aid to the state electing Republican Michael Whatley to the Senate — before claiming he was joking.

"You're waiting for some additional money … and I'm gonna get that to you, Michael," Trump said. "Now, if Michael loses, I'm not sending it. Okay?"

Then Trump added: "No, I'm only kidding. You're getting it. You're gonna get it, Michael."

An AP investigation this year found that blue states had to wait longer for disaster aid and were denied more frequently . (The White House told the AP "there is no politicization to the President's decisions on disaster relief.") And the Energy Department in a July 15 legal filing explicitly acknowledged that it canceled clean-energy grants " based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state " — i.e. whether it "was in a Blue State or a non-Blue State."

It's hard to see how people still recovering from Hurricane Helene don't take this threat somewhat seriously. And regardless of how Trump meant it, this is not really a laughing matter.

The other development this week is Trump's increasingly blunt effort to force the Kennedy Center to take his name . He's been repeatedly denied in court, so he's getting more open about his threats.

Trump said on social media Tuesday that renovations "cannot begin until such time as the DC Circuit rules on the Board's approved name."

"If the ruling is a negative one … the Reconstruction and the Renovation of The Kennedy Center will not take place," he added .

"For me to get involved and to take that on long-term and to carry it or to raise money to carry it — I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition," he told reporters in Charlotte. "Because frankly, if we don't do that, it's going to close. It'll end up being ripped down."

Trump was then pictured on Air Force One on Wednesday night reviewing a poster that appeared to say "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED."

So this is a president now explicitly saying he needs personal recognition to save this institution — and unsubtly threatening its demise if he doesn't get what he wants.

Trump's $5,000 checks idea might be the most brazen.

At the Republican midterm convention last week, Trump said that if Americans reelect GOP congressional majorities, "I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000."

It would be one thing to say that electing Republican majorities would enable the party to pass cut taxes, or something like that. But Trump is expressly tying handing out large sums of cash to people — apparently without congressional approval — as a reward for giving him what he wants.

Even some on the right have labeled that a bribe . It certainly seems like a quid pro quo — a payment made in exchange for a specific outcome.

And imagine if that became the new normal. The only thing stopping presidents from paying ever-larger sums of money for votes might be the economic consequences of doing so.

There is evidence that the American people see through what Trump is doing.

A Reuters-Ipsos poll this week showed 66% of registered voters said that Trump's promise to hand out $5,000 checks if the GOP wins the midterms was "inappropriate," compared to just 18% who said it was appropriate.

Even Republicans leaned toward it being inappropriate, 37%-33%.

And while voters previously tended to view both parties as about equally corrupt, some recent surveys suggest the GOP is suddenly at a deficit on this issue.

A New York Times-Siena College poll this week showed likely voters said by 14 points that "corrupt" described Republicans more than Democrats. And a Fox News poll showed registered voters said Democrats would do a better job on issues of corruption by 11 points.

But Trump doesn't seem to have much regard for this perception. He and his deferential GOP congressional allies have made the presidency too powerful not to squeeze all the juice out of it that he can.

And he'll apparently just keep squeezing.

articles.title: Fox News Poll: Majority says immigration enforcement has crossed the line
articles.summary: A Fox News poll finds Trump's immigration approval at 43%, and 53% of voters say ICE enforcement has gone too far, nearly erasing the GOP's edge.
articles.body: A 53% majority of registered voters say the Trump administration’s enforcement of immigration laws has gone too far, according to new Fox News polling, a view that has stayed consistent since June 2025. The remaining voters are split between enforcement not going far enough and enforcement that's just about right (23% each). The results skew along party lines: 87% of Democrats and 60% of independents say enforcement has gone too far, while most Republicans split between not far enough (40%) and about right (43%). Among those saying enforcement has gone too far, voters are divided on the reason: 45% point to the government using too much force, while 49% say the wrong people are being targeted. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Democrats say the government is targeting the wrong people (by 7 points) while independents say it’s because of using too much force (by 2 points). There are not enough Republicans saying the enforcement has gone too far to draw meaningful conclusions. Consequently, President Trump’s approval rating on immigration sits at 43%, down from a high of 48% last summer. For the past four years, until this summer, voters consistently said the Republicans would do a better job handling immigration than the Democrats. That advantage has all but disappeared, as voters are split between the parties (48% D vs. 49% R). The Democrats are competitive on immigration due to independents backing them over the GOP by 6 points and 15% of non-MAGA Republicans preferring the Democrats. FOX NEWS POLL: COOL YOUR SERVERS! VOTERS REJECT DATA CENTERS "The immigration issue has been defined in terms of border security since the Biden years," says Daron Shaw, the GOP pollster who helps conduct the survey with Democrat Chris Anderson. "But voters now think of immigration policy as ICE crackdowns, and many say these have been too aggressive." Despite fewer than 1 in 10 (8%) voters identifying immigration as their priority, it only trails the cost of living (34%) and the broader economy (14%) as the most important issue facing the country. One more thing… Nearly two-thirds of voters (63%) agree that a child born to an illegal immigrant in the United States should automatically become a citizen. While overall support has softened from previous highs around 67-69%, it’s still far above its low of 45% in 2006. CLICK HERE FOR CROSSTABS AND TOPLINE Again, results are defined by partisanship: roughly 9 in 10 Democrats and 6 in 10 independents support birthright citizenship, while 6 in 10 Republicans oppose it. Among Hispanic voters, two-thirds disapprove of Trump’s overall job performance and his handling of immigration. They trust the Democrats over the Republicans on the issue by 19 points, while 60% say immigration enforcement has gone too far. Three-quarters of Hispanic voters think citizenship should be guaranteed for those born in the U.S. to illegal immigrant parents. Conducted September 11-14, 2026, under the direction of Beacon Research (D) and Shaw & Company Research (R), this Fox News survey includes interviews with a sample of 1,211 registered voters randomly selected from a national voter file. Respondents spoke with live interviewers on landlines (96) and cellphones (821) or completed the survey online after receiving a text (294). Results based on the full sample have a margin of sampling error of ±3 percentage points. Sampling error for results among subgroups is higher. In addition to sampling error, question wording and order can influence results. Weights are generally applied to age, race, education and area variables to ensure the demographics are representative of the registered voter population. Sources for developing weight targets include the most recent American Community Survey, Fox News Voter Analysis and voter file data.

articles.title: Radical El-Sayed ally doubles down on anti-American rhetoric with stunning terrorist comparison
articles.summary: Hasan Piker told Axios that America is worse than al-Qaeda "pound for pound," deepening scrutiny of his ties to Abdul El-Sayed's Michigan Senate race.
articles.body: A popular far-left streamer tied the Democratic nominee in the high-stakes U.S. Senate race in Michigan doubled down on anti-American comments he's made in the past during an on-camera interview released Thursday. Hasan Piker was featured in an episode of "The Axios Show" taped in Los Angeles, where he resides, where interviewer Alex Thompson recalled the internet personality's past claim that "America is the top dog in terrorism." "Do you think America, then, is worse than al-Qaeda?" Thomspon asked. HASAN PIKER INSISTS ABDUL EL-SAYED ASKED HIM TO 'STUMP' FOR MICHIGAN CAMPAIGN AMID BACKLASH "Pound for pound as far as the number of deaths, yes," Piker replied. "We have caused tremendous terror all around the world." "I think that that is not only terror that we are waging on regular civilians, and nations in the periphery, but it's also having consequences on ourselves," the Twitch streamer continued. "It's having dramatic consequences on the home front." "One clear example of this is what we did in Minab [Iran],' Piker said, referring to American attacks earlier this year that struck a school. A United Nations mission said it found "reasonable grounds" to believe that the U.S. committed a war crime. "There's no distinction between blowing up a school, tripple-tapping it with Tomahawk missiles. If you're killing 140 school girls, that is an act of terror." Piker conceded that not all Americans are terrorists, but still called for an "environment of accountability." EL-SAYED PALS AROUND WITH FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER THE DAY BEFORE CRUCIAL MICHIGAN SENATE ELECTION Piker is closely tied to Abdul El-Sayed, the controversial far-left U.S. Senate candidate in Michigan. Piker joined El-Sayed on the campaign trail during primary season. The two were pictured partying together on the night El-Sayed ended up winning his primary election. Since winning the Democratic primary, El-Sayed hasn't been able to shake Piker's shadow, and has refused to condemn him for past controversial comments. Instead the candidate has painting him as a "streamer from California" who has no bearing on the race in Michigan in attempts to distance himself from Piker's more radical views and comments. Piker said in 2019 that "America deserved 9/11." He has also praised Mao Zedong and Communist China, said capitalists should be murdered in the streets and is known for making antisemitic comments. El-Sayed's campaign responded to Piker's comments on The Axios Show, but did not mention Piker by name. ABDUL EL-SAYED DISMISSES QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER TIES ON 'FACE THE NATION,' PIVOTS TO GROCERIES "I do not agree with this statement [on al-Qaeda], nor do I give much weight to the statements made by a social media streamer," the campaign told Axios. "I am more concerned with the dangerous policies of Donald Trump and Mike Rogers that are raising the prices of gas, groceries and healthcare for Michiganders." El-Sayed's campaign reiterated that statement when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP During a trip to Washington, D.C. on Wednesday to meet with potential future colleagues, El-Sayed was caught on camera walking into the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC). When asked by Fox News Digital whether he would condemn Piker, El-Sayed waved off the question and swiftly ducked into the building where he sat down with Democrat senators. El-Sayed's staff later banned Fox News Digital from joining an impromptu post-meeting press event where he took questions and discussed a range of issues key to the 2026 midterms.

articles.title: Senate Democrats, minus Fetterman, urge Hegseth to provide receipt for Iran war costs
articles.summary: All of the Democrats in the Senate — excluding Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman — signed an open letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing him to give Congress a cost breakdown of the war in Iran. The letter, although largely symbolic, reflects the frustration of many Democrats in Congress over what they perceive as a…
articles.body:
All of the Democrats in the Senate — excluding Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman — signed an open letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, pressing him to give Congress a cost breakdown of the war in Iran.

The letter, although largely symbolic, reflects the frustration of many Democrats in Congress over what they perceive as a lack of transparency from the Trump administration about how much taxpayer money the war has cost and how future money Congress allots for the war might be spent.

The senators asked Hegseth to provide a detailed breakdown of the cost of the war to date and future spending requests as well as an account of how unspent dollars from last year will be disbursed by Sept. 30.

“Despite asking for tens of billions of additional taxpayer dollars, you have so far failed to provide basic information on how this money has and will be spent,” the Democratic senators, led by Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, wrote. “Congress must have access to this information to carry out our oversight responsibilities. It is the bare minimum that any American would expect in balancing their own household budget.”

The letter also comes after The Hill reported that Pentagon officials told congressional staff in August that the estimated cost of the war was now at $42 billion.

Fetterman has been a consistent supporter of the war in Iran, putting him at odds with his caucus. He has voted with Republicans against Democratic efforts to condemn the war and criticized his colleagues for their response to the conflict.

“My record has been consistent. I’ve always been at odds with my fellow Democrats over how we hold Iran accountable,” Fetterman said in a statement. “I’ll continue to remain an unapologetic supporter of efforts to confront the Iranian regime and its proxies.”

The other Democrats have homed in on the war’s price tag. In Thursday’s letter, they cited the administration’s multiple requests for more defense funding, including a $67 billion supplemental funding request in June and the $1.5 trillion total funding request from the Pentagon for the next fiscal year.

Those numbers are especially contentious amid deliberations about next year’s government funding, which are currently at a standstill. Republicans want the Defense Department — and especially the war — fully funded, while Democrats insist that the defense total must be lower to allot more money to domestic programs like infrastructure and healthcare.

articles.body:

articles.title: 'Gone too far:' GOP candidate runs to Trump’s left on signature issue in deep red district
articles.summary: María Elvira Salazar tells Trump his immigration enforcement has gone too far, warning that Hispanics who backed him in 2024 now feel betrayed.
articles.body: Rep. María Elvira Salazar, a Republican who represents a solidly red district in Miami, has broken with the president on immigration as the midterms cycle hits a fever pitch. "Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far," Salazar said in a newly released campaign advertisement. "Be careful what your advisors are telling you about immigration policy. The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today. You can be for immigration what Lincoln was for slavery and Reagan was for communism. "I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land." THE HISPANIC VOTE IS UP FOR GRABS IN 2026; CANDIDATES WHO IGNORE IT WILL LOSE A Fox News poll released Wednesday found President Donald Trump’s overall approval rating at 39%, with 61% of registered voters disapproving of his job performance. Voters disapprove of Trump generally by a margin of 61% to 39%, according to the poll. On immigration, however, only 56% of voters are unhappy with the president's performance, beating out his handling of the economy and foreign policy. VOTERS SAY REPUBLICANS OUTDO DEMOCRATS ON THESE KEY ISSUES: FOX NEWS POLL Salazar’s break with the president on immigration follows a legislative record that has combined tougher enforcement measures with support for legal status reforms. During her time in Congress, Salazar has supported tougher border enforcement while also backing legislation that would provide legal status to some long-term noncitizens, including through the bipartisan DIGNITY Act. She also voted for the 2023 Secure the Border Act and the 2025 Laken Riley Act, which expanded immigration enforcement and required the detention of certain undocumented immigrants accused of crimes. TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94% Trump’s hardline stance on immigration, likewise, is nothing new. The issue defined his initial rise to power during the 2016 presidential election, and he leaned heavily into promises of deportations while on the campaign trail in 2024. Amid the president’s hawkish rhetoric, Hispanics in places such as the Miami metropolitan area and along the Southern border shifted heavily to the right. Trump has endorsed Salazar’s bid for re-election. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The Salazar campaign did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Thursday.

articles.title: House GOP lawmaker under fire by fellow Republicans after ad bashing Trump on immigration

I’m not talking about giving them amnesty. I’m talking about giving them a dignified life in this promised land. And only you can do that." TRUMP-BACKED REPUBLICAN SURVIVES PRIMARY AFTER BUCKING HIM ON DEPORTATIONS It’s a notable choice of words, given that her district voted for Trump by double digits in 2024. But she’s one of several Hispanic lawmakers in the House GOP who have been warning their party could be alienating Hispanic and Latino voters who were critical to Republican wins in recent years. Salazar’s South Florida district is rated R+6 by the nonpartisan Cook political report, meaning it’s likely to stay in Republican hands. But Democrats are targeting her seat as a potential pickup opportunity as they work to win back control of the House. She previously took heat from the Freedom Caucus over her bipartisan legislation to reform the asylum process and give a legal pathway to undocumented people already in the U.S. who have not committed crimes. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) also pushed back on Salazar, telling Fox News in a statement, "DHS is focused on delivering the most HISTORIC mass deportation campaign in American history — exactly as President Trump promised. To be clear: The only thing America should be giving illegal aliens is a one-way ticket home or a generous $3,000 check for them to self-deport immediately. We will not ignore the rule of law."

Kennedy fans vaccine injury concerns at anti-vaccine event

Returning to the anti-vaccine group he long chaired on Thursday, Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert. F. Kennedy Jr. Used his keynote address to reinvigorate concerns about vaccine injuries .

© Jacquelyn Martin, Associated Press file

Speaking at an event hosted by Children’s Health Defense, reiterated many of his oft-mentioned arguments, including that he “never heard” of conditions like autism, peanut allergies, eczema and asthma.

The secretary often repeats this anecdote to support his claims that a synthetic factor must be inducing these conditions in children.

He has long supported the claim that vaccines could be linked to autism, though decades of research have yet to establish a clear connection . Critics push back on this claim, arguing detection methods for these conditions have become more sophisticated over time.

“We have a very bad vaccine adverse event reporting system. The only surveillance system that we really rely on to make to add candidates to this list is broken,” Kennedy said. “In fact, CDC’s own study of that system in 2010 — you can look it up, it’s called the Lazarus study — Found that fewer than one percent of vaccine injuries are reported. That means more than 99 percent are not reported.”

The study Kennedy cited did not conclude that 99 percent of vaccine injuries go unreported. The study noted that “fewer than 1% of vaccine adverse events are reported” as context explaining the limitations of a self-reported system like the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System.

In his address, Kennedy took credit for helping “preserve individual choice without federal mandates.” While the federal government makes vaccine recommendations and has previously enacted requirements for certain, broad vaccination requirements for the general public do not exist.

“Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy added.

articles.body:
Nonpartisan election handicapper Cook Political Report shifted Alaska’s gubernatorial race to a toss-up on Thursday after previously leaning Republican.

Jessica Taylor, the handicapper’s Senate and governors editor, reported that new AARP polling found Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins had 40 percent of respondents’ backing, while his closest challenger — conservative businesswoman Bernadette Wilson (R) — garnered 20 percent.

The remaining two candidates, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor (R), polled 14 percent and 7 percent, respectively.

Jessica Taylor wrote that Alaska’s ranked choice voting leaves the GOP vulnerable, as the party fears voters will fail to rank gubernatorial candidates beyond the first pick. The ranking system diminishes the advantages Republicans would have in the race for governor given that there are two on the ballot.

“The AARP poll backs up that fear, finding that a quarter of GOP voters — who overwhelmingly backed Trump by a 41-point margin — simply aren’t ranking anyone in the contest, which is helping Kreiss-Tomkins and hurting Wilson, who was the top Republican vote-getter in the primary,” she continued.

The Cook editor noted that, though Wilson won votes in the primary, the businesswoman has called on Bronson and Treg Taylor to step out of the race and show her support.

“Further voter education from Republicans on the RCV system could help tighten this contest, so we are only moving it into Toss Up for now given the high volatility of a race that’s difficult to game out,” the editor concluded. “But Kreiss-Tomkins is winning independent voters by 34 points, also helping him solidify his frontrunner status.”

The handicapper previously considered the race to replace term-limited Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) as “likely Republican,” shifting away from solidly red, due to the “ranked-choice complexities.”

Democrat Tom Begich dropped from the race in August and backed Kreiss-Tomkins, with both having advanced to the general election in the Last Frontier’s open primary.

articles.title: Postal Service chief says work stopped on computer system key to Trump effort to limit mail voting
articles.summary: WASHINGTON — The top official at the U.S.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — The top official at the U.S. Postal Service said Thursday that the agency has stopped work on developing a controversial computer system that was central to President Donald Trump’s effort to limit mail voting after the Supreme Court rejected his executive order this week. “There’s an injunction, so we’re not doing anything,” Postmaster General David Steiner told The Associated Press in an interview. Steiner, a onetime chief executive of Waste Management, has spent most of the past year atop the Postal Service navigating political and financial challenges. He’s pressing Congress for changes that would help him resolve what he has called a “liquidity crisis.” And Trump’s efforts to largely eradicate mail voting turned the Postal Service into an unlikely arbiter of who is eligible to vote just months before this year’s critical midterm elections, a role Steiner seemingly had little interest in playing. Unlike Trump, who was sharply critical of the Supreme Court decision and ridiculed some of the justices, Steiner offered no assessment of the court’s action. Steiner also declined to take a position on Trump’s policy, presenting himself as the leader of an “independent agency of the executive branch” whose influence over the president’s order was limited to operational concerns. “I don’t get to decide what rules that are put on us that I decide to accept or not accept,” he said. “I looked at it more from the execution side.” The Postal Service has asserted its independence in the past, including during a 2019 standoff when the first Trump administration sought to pressure the agency as the president was in a dispute with Amazon. Steiner said he wouldn’t get into the “nuance” of that. But the pressure has grown so intense at points that it’s fueled talk of whether Steiner might resign, a notion he denied. “There’s no truth to that,” he said. “I think I know the motivation behind it. I think it’s somebody that would like to see me out of a job.” Inserting the Postal Service into elections The executive order Trump signed in March directed several federal agencies to develop state citizenship lists. Those lists would have been delivered to an online portal at the Postal Service, which would have been allowed to send mail ballots only to voters who were cleared through the process. Steiner said he knew about the order about a month before it was unveiled but said his focus was largely on implementation, not the policy’s merits. A whistleblower report released earlier this month by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., argued the system was hastily built and riddled with errors. Steiner said he read “portions” of the whistleblower report and acknowledged the obstacles associated with building such a massive platform quickly. Still, he said he had confidence in colleagues working on the project and had planned to unveil it around Sept. 15. “There’s absolutely no doubt that we worked fast,” he said. “My personal opinion is it was a monumental task, and I’m very proud of our IT department for being able to do it that fast.” In addition to the voter list, Trump’s order would have required states to adopt a uniform envelope style that included barcodes, something states said would have been arduous so close to the election. Following the Supreme Court’s ruling, a memo sent to all Postal Service employees Wednesday and obtained by the AP said the agency will “not be enforcing any of these new rules in the 2026 federal election.” “First and foremost, for Election Mail it is business as usual,” according to the memo. “We continue to follow established protocols, and we remain entirely focused on our core mission: delivering the mail safely and securely for voters and election officials across the country.” Though the Supreme Court rejected Trump’s executive order for this year’s election, Justice Brett Kavanaugh indicated he might rule in favor of the administration if the issue comes back before the court at a later time. Steiner encourages voters to cast ballots early Steiner said the Postal Service would still encourage the use of envelopes and barcodes in future elections, which it has long recommended. He said such changes wouldn’t be required, but those who don’t comply may have to pay more. “If you use the barcode in the envelope, we’ll charge you a lower price,” he said. “If you don’t, we’re going to charge you a higher price because it’s harder for us to process.” While the Postal Service isn’t moving forward on Trump’s order, there are still concerns about postmark delays that could have an impact on this year’s elections. The number of ballots rejected for late postmarks has soared in the vote-by-mail states of Washington and Oregon, according to recently released data highlighting concerns about recent changes in Postal Service operations. Steiner said there were no plans to alter those operations and encouraged voters who use mail to get their ballots in early. “We say seven days,” he said. “Everything is solved if people vote early.”
